<poem>{{smaller block|In this commotion, but the starry cope
Of heaven perhaps, or all the elements
At least had gone to ''wrack'', disturb’d and torn
With violence of this conflict. ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 994.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|<poem>Moaning and wailing for an heir to rule
After him, lest the realm should go to ''wrack''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Coming of Arthur.}}}}

'''wrack<sup>1</sup>†''' (rak), ''v. t.'' [< ''wrack'', ''n.'' Cf. ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] To destroy; make shipwreck of; wreck.
{{smaller block|<poem>What proffits it the well built ship to ride
Vpon the surging billowes of the maine, . . .
If, ere it iornles end it doth attaine, . . .
Sea ''wrackt'' it perish in the raging floud?</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 129.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, what a second ruthless sea of woes
''Wracks'' me within my haven!</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Monsieur D’Olive, i. 1.}}}}

'''wrackful†''' (rak′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wrakeful'', ''wrakful''; < ''wrack''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''. Cf. ''wreckful''.] Ruinous; destructive.

'''wraith''' (rāth), ''n.'' [Appar. an altered form due to some confusion of the dial. ''warth'', an apparition; supposed to have been orig. a guardian spirit, < Icel. ''vörth'' (gen. ''varthar''), a ward, guardian; cf. Norw. ''varde'', a beacon, pile of stones, ''vardyvle'', a guardian or attendant spirit said to go before or follow a man, also considered as an omen or a boding spirit: see ''ward''<sup>1</sup>.] An apparition in the exact likeness of a person, supposed to be seen before or soon after the person’s death; in general, a visible spirit; a specter; a ghost.
{{smaller block|<poem>His presence scared the clan,
Who held him for some fleeting ''wraith'',
And not a man of blood and breath.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 28.}}
In 1799 a traveller writes of the peasants of Kirkcudbrightshire: “It is common among them to fancy that they see the ''wraiths'' of persons dying, which will be visible to one and not to others present with him.”
{{right|''E. B. Tylor'', Prim. Culture, I. 405.}}
<poem>Then glided out of the joyous wood
The ghastly ''Wraith'' of one that I know.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, xxiii.}}}}

'''wrak†''', '''wrake†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' Old spellings of ''wrack''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wramp''' (ramp), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A sprain.

'''wran''' (ran), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''wren''.
{{smaller block|The ''wran!'' the ''wran!'' the king of all birds.
{{right|Quoted in ''N. and Q.'', 1st ser., XII. 489.}}}}

'''wrang'''<sup>1</sup> (rang, locally vrang), ''a.'', ''n.'', and ''adv.'' An obsolete or dialectal (Scotch) form of ''wrong''.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''wrang'''<sup>2</sup>. An obsolete or provincial preterit of ''wring''.

'''wrangle''' (rang′gl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wrangled'', ppr. ''wrangling''. [< ME. ''wranglen;'' a freq. form connected with LG. ''wrangen'', wrangle, Dan. ''vringle'', twist, entangle, and ult. with ''wring:'' see ''wring''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To dispute; argue noisily or in a quarrelsome manner; brawl; altercate.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am ready to distrust mine eyes,
And ''wrangle'' with my reason.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 3. 14.}}
I have been atoning two most ''wrangling'' neighbours.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, iii. 4.}}
<poem>Tho’ among ourselves with too much Heat
We sometimes ''wrangle'', when we should debate.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', To Boileau Despreaux (1704).}}}}
'''2.''' To engage in discussion and disputation; argue; debate; hence, formerly, in some universities, to dispute publicly; defend or oppose a thesis by argument.
{{smaller block|The Philosophers, as they scorne to delight, so must they bee content little to mooue; sauing ''wrangling'' whether Vertue bee the chiefe or the onely good; whether the contemplatiue or the active life doe excell.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 41.}}
<poem>Then, in the scale of reas’ning life, ’tis plain,
There must be, somewhere, such a rank as man:
And all the question (''wrangle'' e’er so long)
Is only this, if God has placed him wrong.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 49.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' To bicker, spar, jangle. See ''quarrel''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''
'''II.†''' ''trans.'' To contest or dispute, especially in the usually brawling manner of the schools.
{{smaller block|Sir Philip, while they ''wrangle'' out their cause, let us agree.
{{right|''Brome'', Northern Lass, v. 8.}}}}

'''wrangle''' (rang′gl), ''n.'' [< ''wrangle'', ''v.''] An angry dispute; a noisy quarrel.
{{smaller block|I have found the court of assistants usually taken up in little ''wrangles'' about coachmen, and adjusting accounts of meal and small-beer.
{{right|''Swift'', Proposal for giving Badges to Beggars.}}}}
={{sc|Syn.}} ''Squabble'', ''Altercation'', etc. (see ''quarrel''<sup>1</sup>), controversy.

'''wrangler''' (rang′glėr), ''n.'' [< ''wrangle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who wrangles or disputes; a debater; especially, an angry or noisy disputant.
{{smaller block|True, true, ever at odds: They were the common talke of the towne for a paire of ''wranglers''.
{{right|''Brome'', Sparagus Garden, i. 1.}}
You should be free and pleasant in every answer and behaviour, rather like well-bred gentlemen in polite conversation than like noisy and contentious ''wranglers''.
{{right|''Watts'', Improvement of Mind, I. xiii. § 20.}}
<poem>I burn to set th’ imprison’d ''wranglers'' free,
And give them voice and utt’rance once again.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 34.}}
As thy great men are fighters and ''wranglers'', so thy mighty things upon the earth and sea are troublesome and intractable incumbrances.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Diogenes and Plato.}}}}
'''2†.''' A stubborn opponent or adversary.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell him he hath made a match with such a ''wrangler''
That all the courts of France will be disturb’d
With chaces.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 264.}}}}
'''3.''' In Cambridge University, one who has attained the first class in the elementary division of the public examination for honors in pure and mixed mathematics, commonly called the ''mathematical tripos'', those who compose the second rank of honors being designated ''senior''

'''2.''' To envelop; surround; cover by winding something round in folds; muffle: often with ''up'': as, to ''wrap up'' a child in its blanket; to ''wrap'' the body in flannels.

'''wrack<sup>1</sup>''' (rak), ''n.''   [Also ''wreck'' (also ''rack''); < ME. ''wrak'', ''wrek'', ''wrec'', something cast ashore, a kind of seaweed, also shipwreck (> F. ''varech'', seaweed cast ashore, pieces of a wrecked ship cast ashore); partly < AS. ''wræc'', banishment, exile, misery; partly < D. LG. ''wrak'', or Icel. ''rek'' (for *''vrek''), also ''reki'', anything drifted or driven ashore, = Sw. ''vrak'', wreck, refuse, trash, = Dan. ''vrag'', wreck. ''Wrack''<sup>1</sup> is a doublet of ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>; it is also spelled in some uses ''rack'', while on the other hand ''rack''<sup>1</sup> was sometimes spelled ''wrack''. Indeed the whole series of words, ''wrack'', ''wreck'', ''rack'', ''reck'', ''wretch'', etc., were formerly much confused in spelling. See ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' That which is cast ashore by the waves. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Seaweed cast ashore. The name is sometimes restricted to the species of ''Fucus'', which form the bulk of the wrack collected for manure and sometimes for making kelp. Those found most plentifully on the shores of the British islands are ''F. vesiculosus'' and ''F. nodosus''. See ''sea-wrack'', 2, and cut under ''Fucus''. (''b'') Wreckage.}}

'''2†.''' The destruction of a ship by winds or rocks or by the force of the waves; shipwreck. See ''wreck''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Ring the alarum-bell! Blow wind! come ''wrack!''
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 5. 51.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nay, some of them . . . run ashore before the pursuer, glad that with ''wrack'' of ship and losse of goods they may prolong a despised life.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 2.}}}}

'''3.''' Destruction; ruin.
{{smaller block|Forgetting shame’s pure blush and honour’s ''wrack.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 558.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nor only Paradise}}

{{smaller block|True, true, ever at odds: They were the common talke of the towne for a paire of ''wranglers''.

'''3.''' In Cambridge University, one who has attained the first class in the elementary division of the public examination for honors in pure and mixed mathematics, commonly called the ''mathematical tripos'', those who compose the second rank of honors being designated ''senior optimes'', and those of the third order ''junior optimes''. {{smaller|The student taking absolutely the first place in the mathematical tripos used to be called the ''senior wrangler'', those following next in the same division being respectively termed ''second, third, fourth'', etc., ''wranglers''. But in the final examination now, to which only wranglers are admitted, the names are arranged in divisions alphabetically. The name is derived from the public disputations in which candidates for degrees were until recent times required to exhibit their powers. Compare ''tripos''.}}

{{smaller block|Maule was senior ''wrangler'' and senior medallist at Cambridge, and is a lawyer. {{right|''Greville'', Memoirs, Jan. 2, 1831.}}}}

'''wranglership''' (rang′glėr-ship), ''n.''   [< ''wrangler'' + ''-ship''.]   In Cambridge University, the position or rank of a wrangler.

'''wranglesome''' (rang′gl-sum), ''a.''   [< ''wrangle'' + ''-some''.]   Contentious; quarrelsome.   ''Halliwell.''

'''wrangling''' (rang′gling), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wranglinge, wranglyng''; verbal n. of ''wrangle, v.'']   Disputation; especially, contentious argumentation.

{{smaller block|Much ''wrangling'' they had, but at last they confirmed him according to promise eight shares of Land; and so he was dismissed of his charge, with shew of fauour and much friendship. Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 132.}}

{{smaller block|We may read what ''wrangling'' the Bishops and Monks had about the reading or not reading of Origen.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}

'''wrangous†''' (rang′us), ''a.'' A Scotch form of ''wrongous''.

'''wrap'''<sup>1</sup> (rap), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wrapped'' or ''wrapt'', ppr. ''wrapping''.   [E. dial. transposed ''warp''; < ME. ''wrappen'', also ''wlappen'' (with ''l'' for ''r''), > E. ''lap'': see ''lap''<sup>3</sup>, and cf. ''envelop'', ''develop''.]   '''1.''' To roll or fold together, as a pliable or flexible object: usually with the preposition ''around'' (or ''round'') or ''about'': as, to ''wrap'' paper ''about'' a book.
{{smaller block|<poem>This said, he took his mantle’s foremost part,
He gan the same together fold and ''wrap''. ''Fairfax.''</poem>
<poem>Like one who ''wraps'' the drapery of his couch
''About'' him, and lies down to pleasant dreams.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Thanatopsis.}}}}
'''2.''' To envelop; surround; cover by winding something round in folds; muffle: often with ''up'': as, to ''wrap up'' a child in its blanket; to ''wrap'' the body in flannels.
{{smaller block|<poem>As a weiȝh woful he ''wrapped'' him ther-inne,
For no man that he met his mornyng schuld knowe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 746.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Sarazines ''wrappen'' here Hedes in white lynnene Clothe. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I, . . . ''wrapp’d'' in mist
Of midnight vapour, glide secure.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 158.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The mother . . .
Then brought a mantle down and ''wrapt'' her in it.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}} '''3.''' To cover and fasten securely, as in paper or pack-sheet, in order to protect from injury or injurious exposure, as in transit or during storage, or in order to conceal: generally with ''up:'' as, to ''wrap up'' an umbrella or a book to send by express; to ''wrap up'' one’s things in a bundle.—'''4.''' To conceal by involving or enveloping; hide in a mass of different character; cover up or involve generally.
{{smaller block|In these fewe lines I haue ''wrapped'' vp the most tedious part of Grammer. {{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|The evil which is here ''wrapt'' up. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 117.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wrapping'' up Religion in strange figures and mysterious non-sense, which the Egyptians were so much given to. {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. iii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Wrapped up in.''' (''a'') Bound up with or in; comprised or involved in; entirely associated with or dependent on.}}
{{smaller block|His [Leontine’s] young wife (''in'' whom all his happiness was ''wrapt up'') died. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 123.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Engrossed in or with; entirely devoted to: as, she is ''wrapped up in'' her son; he is ''wrapped up in'' his studies.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O then, O, first for your own royal sake,
And next for ours, ''wrapp’d up in'' you, beware
Of his Designs in time. ''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, v. 152.</poem>
The state pedant is ''wrapt up in'' news, and lost in politics. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 105.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Comprised or involved in, as an effect or consequence.}}

'''wrap'''<sup>1</sup> (rap), ''n.''   [< ''wrap''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   An article of dress intended to be wrapped round the person, as on a journey; a wrapper. {{smaller|In the plural, the word is applied collectively to all coverings used, in addition to the usual clothing, as a defense against the weather, as cloaks, shawls, scarfs, and railway-rugs. Mrs. Aleshine . . . was sitting in her bonnet and ''wraps'', ready to start forth. {{right|''F. R. Stockton'', The Dusantes, iii.}}}}

'''wrap<sup>2</sup>†''' (rap), ''v. t.'' A misspelling of ''rap''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>The least of these delights, that you devise,
Able to ''wrape'' and dazzle human eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Peele'', Arraignment of Paris, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wrapp’d'' in amaze, the matrons wildly stare.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, v. 840.}}}}

'''wrappage''' (rap′ạ̄j), ''n.''   [< ''wrap''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age''.]   '''1.''' The act of wrapping.—'''2.''' Anything which wraps, or is used for wrapping; collectively, things used as wraps or wrappers.
{{smaller block|It seems somehow the very central essence of us, Song; as if all the rest were but ''wrappages'' and hulls! {{right|''Carlyle'', Heroes and Hero-Worship, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hence was the need, on either side, of a lie
To serve as decent ''wrappage''.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, iv. 523.}}}}
{{smaller block|To-morrow this sheet . . . shall be the ''wrappage'' to a bar of soap, or the platter for a beggar’s broken victuals. {{right|''Lowell'', Biglow Papers, 1st ser., vi., note.}}}}

'''wrapper''' (rap′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wrap''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who wraps.—'''2.''' That in which anything is wrapped or inclosed; an outer covering: as, newspaper ''wrappers''.
{{smaller block|As soon as such a number of books are perfected, the surplus of the various signatures are thrown aside for ''wrappers'' and other official uses. {{right|''Rev. W. Tooke'', in Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 430.}}}}
{{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') The loose and detachable cover of paper put about a book bound in cloth to preserve its freshness; sometimes, incorrectly, the sewed or pasted cover of a pamphlet. (''b'') Tobacco-leaf specially suited or prepared for covering cigars: distinguished from ''filler''. See ''filler''<sup>1</sup>, 4.}}

{{smaller block|Sumatra tobacco consists of large, strong, flexible leaves, which are imported into this country solely for the purpose of making cigar ''wrappers''.
{{right|''The Nation'', XLVIII. 379.}}}}

'''3.''' A loose garment meant to envelop the whole, or nearly the whole, person: applied to both indoor and outdoor garments, such as dressing-gowns, overcoats, and shawls. {{smaller|At certain times}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
